summary: Real, costly pain for 1–10 unit landlords, but it is a once-per-move-out purchase with no first-person demand evidence, crowded free templates, and ChatGPT as a close substitute. Cheap to build, yet the paid wedge over free tools is unproven and reach is weak.

demand.evidence: RESEARCH.md found no first-person landlord complaints; all pain evidence is law-firm and vendor blog content (verticalrent, landlordstudio), and the stats (40% of small claims, 68% of renters) are second-hand. Competitor pricing (TurboTenant $119/yr, ProofMi $39–$119/yr) shows landlords pay for adjacent tools, not for this. No one has asked for it or paid.

statusQuo.evidence: Landlords use free templates (Landlord Studio, Paperform), a lawyer, or ChatGPT with a pasted statute, per RESEARCH.md. The workaround is cheap and mostly good enough for the letter; the real gap (state deadline, proration, evidence) is a correctness risk landlords may not feel until they lose a case.

specificity.evidence: Buyer is a self-managing 1–10 unit landlord at move-out, a concrete moment with a real consequence (2–3x deposit plus fees). But there is no named person or quote; 'accidental landlord' is still a category, and they handle 1–4 move-outs a year, so they are hard to find and reach.

wedge.evidence: Deadline + receipt-rule check + prorated line items + PDF for five states is a clean, deterministic, weekend-sized wedge, and $19 per packet is easy to price-test. Weakness: the free preview of the same calculation may be all they need.

futureFit.evidence: General AI will keep improving at drafting letters, shrinking the template value; the durable part is a maintained, verified statute table and stored evidence, which carries ongoing liability and upkeep. Purchase is episodic with low repeat rate.

premises: Small landlords lose money or cases from missed deadlines and unprorated deductions — supported by law-firm and vendor sources, not by landlords' own words.
They will pay $19 for correctness when free templates and ChatGPT exist — unsupported; no evidence.
A state-rule table for five states can be kept accurate enough to avoid liability — plausible but a real ongoing cost and risk.
Landlords can be reached at the move-out moment through search or communities — weak; search is crowded with free templates.
alternatives: Minimal: free state deadline + proration calculator page as SEO and email capture, with the paid PDF added only if the calculator gets traffic.
Ideal: annual plan with reminders, a move-in evidence vault and 50 states — heavier, needs a maintained legal table, and is a different product.
Lateral: sell to small property managers or as an embed/affiliate to TurboTenant-style suites rather than direct to landlords.
Extend an existing repo: none close in the portfolio; ownerbrief and covercheck serve different users.
wedge: A free-to-preview, $19-to-download prorated, state-checked itemized statement for CA/TX/FL/NY/WA with a deadline countdown.

feasibility.notes: Next.js on Vercel with a static rules table, a proration function and pdf-lib. The one test that proves M1: the roadmap's deadline cases (CA 2026-03-22, TX 2026-03-31, NY 2026-03-15), the 300.00 proration and the 1550.00 refund all pass. Statute accuracy is the real work, not the code.

risks: Free templates and ChatGPT cover most of the value
Wrong statute data could harm users and create unauthorized-practice-of-law exposure
Search keywords are crowded and landlord communities dislike promotion
killCriteria: Drop if, after two weeks in landlord communities and search, fewer than 50 relevant visitors, under 5% waitlist/start rate, or no one answers a price question at $19; or if testers say ChatGPT with the statute is good enough.
